Week 39: A Week of Standoff, Not Collapse

Executive power pushed harder against courts, Congress, and the press this week, but nearly every push met resistance that mostly held.

Week 39 opens with a government still shut down, and a president still testing how far executive power can reach before someone with authority says no. What emerges is not one dramatic act but many small ones, arriving from different directions in the same seven days. Judges said no, repeatedly. The administration answered by appealing, escalating, or simply proceeding elsewhere. The Democracy Clock, which tracks this grinding contest, barely moved this week. Its stillness conceals a week of unusual density and consequence.

At the close of Week 38, the clock stood at 7:42 p.m. It now reads 7:41 p.m., a shift of six seconds, essentially a holding pattern. That near-flatness reflects two forces pulling against each other with similar weight. Executive assertion intensified across military deployment, civil service purges, prosecutorial retaliation, and press suppression. But courts, in unusual numbers and across the ideological spectrum, kept ruling the administration's actions unlawful. The stillness on the clock face is not peace; it is a standoff.

The most direct test of that standoff involved soldiers in American cities. Trump ordered National Guard troops into Chicago, Portland, Memphis, and Washington, over the objections of local officials, using Title 10 and Title 32 authority meant for emergencies. Federal judges disagreed with his account of the emergency. Judge April Perry in Illinois issued a fourteen-day injunction, finding the government's justification incredible. Judge Karin Immergut in Oregon, a Trump appointee, ruled that the administration's factual claims about Portland were "untethered to reality." Judge Charles Breyer had already found, days earlier, that the Los Angeles deployment violated the Posse Comitatus Act outright.

The administration did not accept these rulings as final. It appealed to the Seventh and Ninth Circuits, winning a partial stay in one venue while losing outright in another. When the Seventh Circuit unanimously rejected the government's claim of unreviewable discretion, the Justice Department filed an emergency shadow-docket appeal to the Supreme Court, seeking to bypass four consecutive losses in a single stroke. Trump, meanwhile, kept alive the possibility of invoking the Insurrection Act, a step that would let him override the courts entirely rather than litigate around them. The pattern was plain: block, appeal, escalate, threaten to leap past the whole judicial apparatus.

Immigration enforcement showed the same instinct toward force, and met less friction along the way. Operation Midway Blitz intensified raids in Chicago. An ICE agent shot and killed a thirty-eight-year-old father during a traffic stop. Agents fired pepper balls at faith leaders and detained a journalist covering the operation. A man exonerated after decades in prison was detained again on a vacated deportation order. A green-card holder was fined for lacking papers under a law rarely enforced. Courts stepped in where they could, blocking warrantless arrests in Illinois and ordering agents to wear body cameras after documented violations of an earlier restraining order. Still, the incidents piled up faster than the remedies.

The shutdown itself became a weapon rather than merely a crisis to be resolved. Russell Vought announced mass layoffs of federal workers, more than four thousand notices across seven agencies, using the funding lapse as legal cover for firings that would otherwise draw immediate challenge. The Pentagon diverted roughly eight billion dollars in research funds to cover military payroll, without new congressional authorization. The administration withheld more than twenty-seven billion dollars in appropriated funds from Democratic-led districts while sparing Republican ones nearly entirely, and canceled Gateway Tunnel funding for New Jersey just ahead of that state's gubernatorial election. Judge Susan Illston blocked the layoffs as illegal, and a second court extended that block days later. The rulings were real checks. But the firings had already gone out, and the fund withholding continued regardless.

Congress, for its part, could barely be called a functioning body this week. The House met only twelve of the prior eighty days. Speaker Johnson refused for weeks to seat Representative-elect Adelita Grijalva, an elected member from Arizona, delaying her chance to sign a discharge petition on the Epstein files. Arizona's attorney general sued to force the swearing-in, calling the delay taxation without representation. The Senate failed its ninth and tenth votes to end the shutdown. Trump told Republican senators to boycott negotiations with Democrats altogether. Johnson admitted publicly that the GOP had no plan to reopen the government or address health coverage costs. This was not gridlock in the ordinary sense. It was the visible absence of a legislature doing its job.

Ahead of a planned nationwide demonstration called No Kings, House Republican leadership mounted a coordinated campaign to discredit it before it happened. Speaker Johnson called it a "hate America" rally. Colleagues branded participants as Antifa, Hamas-aligned, Marxist, and secretly funded by George Soros. Fox News echoed the framing. Senator Ted Cruz proposed legislation to let the Justice Department pursue RICO charges against the protest's funders, turning an organized-crime statute into a weapon against political organizing. White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt went further, describing the Democratic Party's own constituency as terrorists, illegal aliens, and violent criminals. None of this was subtle. It was an open attempt to redefine mass peaceful assembly as a security threat before a single person had marched.

Retaliation against individual critics deepened alongside the rhetoric against protesters. Trump publicly called for investigations of Adam Schiff, James Comey, Christopher Wray, John Bolton, Lisa Monaco, and Andrew Weissmann. Bolton was indicted on eighteen counts tied to classified information, in a case that had previously been dropped and was later reopened. IRS official Gary Shapley compiled a list of Democratic donors as investigative targets. Stephen Miller led coordinated social-media attacks on a federal judge who had ruled against the administration. El Salvador's Nayib Bukele publicly urged Trump to impeach American judges who ruled against him, a call amplified by MAGA-aligned figures at home. None of these were isolated flashes of anger. Together they described a strategy: turn prosecution and public pressure against anyone positioned to check or criticize the administration.

The press itself absorbed one of the week's sharpest blows. The Pentagon imposed new credentialing rules requiring reporters to pledge not to seek unauthorized information, in effect demanding pre-clearance for unclassified reporting. Nearly every major outlet refused to sign; only OAN accepted the terms. Even The Australian, an international paper, withdrew its earlier assent after reviewing the implications. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell dismissed the departing press corps as "self-righteous" and announced a replacement roster drawn from friendlier outlets. This was not censorship achieved through force. It was censorship achieved through terms so restrictive that independent journalism chose to walk away, leaving the government to fill the vacuum with voices it had already vetted.

Reproductive and voting rights absorbed simultaneous pressure this week, arriving from different directions but landing in the same place. The Justice Department announced it would no longer enforce the FACE Act, which protects access to abortion clinics. Trump ended federal protection for emergency abortion care, signed an executive order requiring proof of citizenship for voter registration, and pardoned twenty-three people convicted of anti-abortion violence. The DOJ dismissed voting rights lawsuits in Georgia, Texas, and Arizona the same week the Supreme Court heard oral arguments in Louisiana v. Callais, with the conservative majority appearing open to weakening Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act substantially. North Carolina Republicans announced plans for further mid-decade gerrymandering. None of these actions stood alone. Together, they described a coordinated retreat from decades of civil rights enforcement, arriving just as the doctrinal foundation for that enforcement faces its own possible unraveling at the Court.

Personal enrichment and foreign entanglement ran through the week as a quieter but persistent thread. Trump promoted a triumphal arch monument near the Potomac while soliciting corporate donations to help pay for it. He held a million-dollar-per-person fundraiser at Mar-a-Lago even as federal workers went unpaid. Foreign investment in Trump-linked ventures, from Gulf states and elsewhere, continued to track suspiciously close to favorable policy outcomes, including arms sales and chip export approvals. Presidential envoy Steve Witkoff was reported to have coached a Russian official on how to manage an upcoming call between Trump and Zelenskyy. Trump then reversed course on providing Tomahawk missiles to Ukraine after speaking with Putin. Each item alone might be dismissed as coincidence. Together, they described a presidency whose foreign policy choices sit uncomfortably close to its financial ones.

Not every event this week ran in the same direction. Admiral Alvin Holsey resigned as head of U.S. Southern Command after reportedly raising legal concerns about lethal strikes on suspected drug vessels in the Caribbean, an unusual departure suggesting friction inside the military over the legality of its own operations. Brown, Penn, and USC all rejected a federal higher-education funding compact that would have traded money for policy concessions. More than three hundred forty former intelligence officials issued a public warning that the country was moving toward what they called competitive authoritarianism. These were not victories in any conventional sense. But they showed that individual and institutional refusal remained possible, even under sustained pressure.

The week's most consequential item may prove to be the one still pending. The Supreme Court's emergency review of the Chicago Guard deployment appeal was unresolved as the week closed, alongside the still-undecided fate of Louisiana v. Callais and the Texas redistricting case. Each carries the power to validate or curtail the pattern this week made visible.

Viewed from a distance, Week 39 marked neither a single collapse nor a single victory. It marked the ordinary machinery of a contest still underway: courts checking, the executive testing the edges of those checks, both sides treating the outcome as unsettled rather than concluded. The mass walkout of the Pentagon press corps, the reopened indictment of a prominent critic, the withheld appropriations, the Guard troops moving from city to city under contested legal theories: all of it describes a government leaning harder against its own restraints, in a week when those restraints, for the most part, still held. Whether they continue to hold is not a question this week answers. It is a question the next one inherits.
